title.en: Evidence, regulation and compliance · three lessons

description.en: Lesson 7.1 Grading the evidence behind an aesthetic claim · Lesson 7.2 Compounding law, the 40-amino-acid line and certificates of analysis · Lesson 7.3 Cosmetic, compounded or investigational: consent and the chart.

unit.tutorContext: Module 7 closes the course: evidence appraisal, US regulatory frameworks and prescriber compliance, kept in separate registers. GRADE: certainty (high, moderate, low, very low; the guides print A–D) for one outcome across a body of evidence, never for a molecule; RCTs start high, observational studies low; rate down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness (study PICO differs from the question), imprecision (CI crosses the important difference) and publication bias (suspect it when evidence is small industry-funded studies); rate up for large effects. Course examples: GHK-Cu's one indexed RCT measured post-laser healing (indirect for photoageing); BPC-157 wound data are rodent (indirect); LL-37 34-person positive then 148-person negative phase IIb (inconsistent); oral collagen benefit only in low-quality and industry-funded trials (risk of bias, Myung 2025). Lundh 2017 Cochrane: industry-sponsored studies more often favourable efficacy results, RR 1.27 (1.17–1.37). Grade and legal status are separate checks; mechanism never raises a grade. US 503A (21 USC 353a): identified patient, prescription; exempt only from approval, adequate directions, cGMP; bulk substance must meet a USP/NF monograph, else be an approved-drug component, else be on the 503A bulks list; registered manufacturer and valid COA; no statutory purity figure. 21 CFR 216.23: six substances, none a peptide, unchanged since 2019 (eCFR current 22 Sep 2026); listing is no endorsement. Categories 1–3 = interim enforcement posture: Category 1 includes non-injectable GHK-Cu (14 May 2026); 503A Category 2 has six substances; BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37, melanotan II are withdrawn nominations with safety concerns still posted. PCAC 23–24 Jul 2026 is advisory; FDA staff concluded criteria weigh against listing BPC-157; only rulemaking changes the list. 503B: registered outsourcing facility, cGMP, risk-based inspection, adverse-event reporting, may compound without patient-specific prescriptions; products unapproved. >40 alpha amino acids = protein = biological product since 23 Mar 2020 (85 FR 10057); tesamorelin and hyaluronidase became BLAs; biologics cannot use 503A/503B exemptions; retatrutide residue count upheld by a district court in 2025, appeal pending (June 2026 filings). COA = supplier's report on one lot: MS identity (observed vs expected mass), HPLC purity (impurities unnamed), endotoxin (limit calculated from dose and route, FDA 2026 guidance), microbial, water, counter-ion, metals, solvents; cannot prove the vial is that lot, storage, sterility or legality; red flags = no lot, no chromatogram, no impurities, no endotoxin on an injectable, over 12 months old. FDA's BPC-157 briefing: public COAs mostly purity only; the nominator's COA reported no endotoxin test, and the COAs supplied were for the acetate while the free base was nominated. Ashraf 2024: three online semaglutide vials 7.7–14.4% purity vs 99% labelled, endotoxin in all. RUO: 21 CFR 312.160 permits shipment for lab or in-vitro research, 'Not for use in humans'; intended use judged objectively (21 CFR 201.128); a COA cannot convert RUO into a pharmaceutical. Cosmetic vs drug by intended use ('regenerate cells' is a drug claim; 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning); supplements not approved before sale; off-label applies only to approved drugs; unapproved new drug in interstate commerce is a prohibited act (21 USC 331); FDA's 2020 warning letter named compounded BPC-157 and GHK-Cu. Chart: article and status in those words; pathway, facility and COA if compounded; consent (not approved, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives incl. nothing, what happens if harm; elements borrowed from 21 CFR 50.25); grade quoted; monitoring and stopping rule; dated status check. UK (checked 25 Sep 2026; moments m7-p21, m7-p22): no 503A/503B; unlicensed medicines reach patients as regulation 167 'specials' (unsolicited order; doctor, dentist, nurse or pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber; one patient's special needs; no advertising; manufacturer's specials licence, GMP-inspected site, product otherwise unassessed) or pharmacy preparation against a prescription (Medicines Act 1968 s.10); MHRA GN14 order: UK-licensed (even off-label) → licensed abroad → UK special → non-medicines such as supplements; special need excludes cost and convenience; prescriber responsible (GMC 102–108, MHRA DSU 2009, GPhC 2025, NMC Code 18). MHRA classifies by claims (websites, social media), form (injection) and use (GN8); no sale, supply or advertising without a UK marketing authorisation (HMR regs 46, 279); injectable melanotan = medicine (FOI 24/274); May 2026 seizure included peptide products; no POM advertising to the public (reg 284, CAP 12.12; Blue Guide: clinics may promote 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' without naming the POM; ASA 11 Feb 2026 Voy ruling on '#mounjaro' posts); GMC: physical examination before prescribing injectable cosmetic medicines. Never give doses, reconstitution, stacking, administration or sourcing; never validate a vendor or call a COA 'safe'. Adapt 'what you do next' to prescriber, clinical staff or advisor without changing grades or facts. The course is designed toward future CME accreditation; no credit is offered at this time.

body.en: This last module turns the course into three habits. You will rate the certainty behind a claim with GRADE, read a compounding status and a certificate of analysis for what they do and do not prove, and write the consent and chart note that an unapproved product needs. The regulatory detail is given for the US in the lesson text, and for the UK, the EU, Portugal, Brazil and the UAE in each moment's regulatory note; lesson 7.2 covers the routes for unlicensed medicines and the rules on selling and advertising peptides outside the US.

videoTranscript.en: This last module turns the course into three habits. You will rate the certainty behind a claim with GRADE, read a compounding status and a certificate of analysis for what they do and do not prove, and write the consent and chart note that an unapproved product needs. Every claim you hear about a skin peptide carries a hidden question. How sure can we be? GRADE answers it with four levels of certainty, from high to very low. The rating belongs to a body of evidence for one outcome, such as wrinkle depth at twelve weeks, and never to a single study or to the molecule itself. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low. From there, certainty drops for five reasons you can name, which are risk of bias, inconsistency between trials, indirectness, imprecision, and suspected publication bias. Both Hormonaly guides print a letter from A to D beside each use. Read those letters as the same four levels, adapted. They rate the evidence for that use, and they say nothing about whether a product is legal.

title.en: GRADE rates certainty in an effect, one outcome at a time.

body.en: GRADE sorts the evidence on a specific question into four levels of certainty: high, moderate, low and very low. The rating applies to a body of evidence for one outcome, never to a single study or to a molecule. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low; certainty then falls for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias, and occasionally rises for a very large effect. Both Hormonaly guides print the letters A to D for the same idea, adapted, and attach each letter to a specific use.

points.en: Four levels, applied to a body of evidence
Five named reasons to rate down
The letter belongs to a use, never to a molecule

blocks.sourceNote: Guyatt 2008 · Balshem 2011 · Core GRADE 2025 · Hormonaly guides

body.en: High, moderate, low, very low: how confident you can be that an estimated effect is close to the truth, for one outcome, across all the studies that address it.
Randomized trials start at high certainty and observational studies at low. The starting point then moves, for reasons you can name.
A to D in both Hormonaly guides maps onto the same four levels. The letter rates the evidence for a listed use. It does not rate legality, popularity or mechanism.

body.en: A Cochrane methodology review brought together 75 papers, each comparing studies sponsored by the manufacturer with studies funded in other ways. Industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results and favourable conclusions, and the difference was not explained by the usual risk-of-bias checks. It is the pattern you met with oral collagen in module 04.

label.en: risk ratio for a favourable efficacy result, industry-sponsored versus other studies

detail.en: Lundh et al., Cochrane 2017 · 95% CI 1.17–1.37 · moderate-certainty evidence

means.en: When a manufacturer pays for the trial, a favourable result is more likely. Funding is a reason to read a trial harder and to look for independent replication.

doesNot.en: It does not make a sponsored trial wrong or an independent one right. It describes an average tilt across many studies and says nothing about any single product.

body.en: GRADE names the ways a body of evidence can mislead. Read the four you will use most. Then sort four cases from this course by the reason that most lowers certainty. The fifth, publication bias, is suspected when the evidence is a handful of small, mostly commercially funded studies.

blocks.sourceNote: Core GRADE 2–5 (BMJ 2025) · Miller 2006 · Grönberg 2014 · Mahlapuu 2021 · Myung 2025 · Seiwerth 2021

note.en: Flaws in design or conduct that can exaggerate an effect; check whether low- and high-quality trials disagree
Unexplained differences in results between studies of the same question
The studies differ from your question in population, intervention, comparison or outcome
Too few people or events; the confidence interval spans an important effect and little or none

callout.en: Name the reason and you can explain a grade to a patient in one sentence.

prompt.en: One case at a time: which reason most lowers certainty here?

label.en: Topical GHK-Cu: the only indexed trial measured healing after laser resurfacing. Your patient asks about photoageing.

why.en: Indirectness. The trial's outcome, healing after resurfacing, is a neighbour of your patient's question, photoageing, so it answers a different question.

label.en: LL-37 in venous leg ulcers: a 34-person trial was positive; a 148-person multicentre trial was negative in its full cohort.

why.en: Inconsistency. Two randomized trials of the same question point in different directions, and the larger one found no effect overall.

label.en: Oral collagen: the pooled benefit disappears when only high-quality trials are kept.

why.en: Risk of bias. When low- and high-quality trials disagree, GRADE gives the high-quality ones the weight, and here they show no effect.

label.en: BPC-157 for skin healing: the wound data come from animal models, mostly rodents.

why.en: Indirectness. The population is animals and your question is about people, as indirect as evidence gets.

done.en: Four placed. Two were indirectness: real studies that answer a different question from the one in front of you. Imprecision comes back in the question that closes this lesson.

body.en: Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate axes, and both Hormonaly guides ask you to clear both. An approved drug can carry a low grade for the use a patient wants, and a compound with stronger human data can still have no lawful route. A plausible mechanism never raises a grade. Say the outcome, the grade and who ran the trials, then check the status as its own step.

points.en: Grade: certainty for this outcome
Status: what the law allows, checked separately
Mechanism never raises a grade

body.en: Name the outcome the patient cares about, the certainty for it, and who paid for the trials behind it.
Check what the product legally is as a separate step. A good grade never makes a product lawful, and an approval says nothing about the grade for an unapproved use.
A persuasive mechanism leaves the grade where it is. Both Hormonaly guides say so in almost the same words.

audioScript.en: Suppose a patient asks whether a peptide works. Start with the outcome they care about, say fewer lines around the eyes, and give the certainty for that outcome, along with who paid for the trials behind it. Then, as a separate step, check what the product legally is. The Hormonaly guides keep these two checks apart for a reason. An approved drug can carry a low grade for the particular use a patient has in mind, and a compound with stronger human data may still have no lawful route in the United States. A persuasive mechanism leaves the grade exactly where it is. Whatever your role, say the outcome and the grade in one breath, and treat the regulatory answer as a question of its own.

prescriber.en: Before you recommend or prescribe, write the outcome and its grade in the note, and record the product's regulatory status on a separate line. If no trial addresses the outcome the patient wants, say so and record it.

clinical-staff.en: When a patient quotes a result, note which outcome it was and where it came from, and pass questions about grades and status to the prescriber rather than rating the product yourself.

advisor.en: Describe what a product has been shown to do, for which outcome, and who funded the trials. Leave the question of whether it can lawfully be prescribed to a prescriber.

title.en: Two compounding routes, one strict order.

body.en: In the US, section 503A lets a licensed pharmacist or physician compound for an identified patient on a prescription, exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and good manufacturing practice. The bulk substance must meet a USP or NF monograph; failing that, be a component of an approved drug; failing that, appear on FDA's 503A bulks list. It must also come from an FDA-registered establishment with a valid certificate of analysis. Section 503B outsourcing facilities register with FDA, work to good manufacturing practice under inspection, and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions.

points.en: 503A: patient-specific, three exemptions
Monograph, then approved component, then the bulks list
503B: registered, inspected, held to good manufacturing practice

blocks.sourceNote: 21 U.S.C. 353a and 353b · FDA 503A bulks page (updated 14 May 2026) · FDA, information for outsourcing facilities

body.en: A licensed pharmacist or physician compounds for an identified patient on a valid prescription. Meeting the conditions exempts the product from approval, adequate directions and good manufacturing practice, and from nothing else.

Monograph first. Only if none exists, a component of an approved drug. Only if neither applies, the 503A bulks list. A valid certificate of analysis and a registered manufacturer are conditions as well.
Outsourcing facilities register with FDA, meet good manufacturing practice, are inspected on a risk-based schedule and report adverse events. Their products remain unapproved.

audioScript.en: Two routes exist for compounding in the United States, and the difference between them shapes the rest of this lesson. Under section 503A, a licensed pharmacist or physician prepares a drug for an identified patient on a prescription. If the conditions are met, the product escapes three requirements, namely approval as a new drug, labelling with adequate directions, and good manufacturing practice. The conditions start with the substance itself, taken in strict order. A USP or National Formulary monograph comes first. Only when there is none can it be a component of an approved drug, and only when neither applies can it sit on FDA's 503A bulks list. The substance must also come from a registered manufacturer with a valid certificate of analysis. Section 503B outsourcing facilities work differently. They register with FDA, work to good manufacturing practice, face risk-based inspection, and can compound without a prescription for each patient. Their products remain unapproved.

text.en: In the EU, medicines prepared in a pharmacy on prescription for an individual patient (magistral formulas) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formulas) are outside Directive 2001/83/EC (Article 3). Pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies are also exempt from manufacturing authorisation (Article 40(2)).

In Portugal, a magistral formula is prepared in a community or hospital pharmacy on a medical prescription naming the patient, under a pharmacist's responsibility (Decreto-Lei 95/2004). Compounded medicines may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese or European pharmacopoeia, another European pharmacopoeia or compendial scientific documentation, and one containing any other raw material may not be prescribed.

In Brazil, a magistral preparation is made individually by a pharmacy against a prescription from an authorised professional (RDC 96/2008). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that any substance must have passed efficacy and safety assessment before it can be compounded, and that compounding may take place only individually, on a medical prescription, in a pharmacy licensed by local health surveillance.

In the UAE, where the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has regulated medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies are exempt from marketing approval under Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 (Art. 5(2)), although such a pharmacy may not copy an EDE-approved product unless no commercial product can deliver the expected benefit, nor formulate products for research, development or experimentation (Art. 95). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) treats peptides as high-risk substances and lets novel substances of unknown risk be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits prescribing, dispensing or using any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026).

title.en: A short list, three categories and a withdrawn table.

body.en: Dated to FDA's records as checked in September 2026. The bulks list is law, changed only by rulemaking; the categories are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated. Neither is an approval.

note.en: Unchanged since 2019. Listing carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.
FDA does not intend to act against compounders who meet its conditions. GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes is here (list of 14 May 2026).
Six substances under 503A as of 14 May 2026, kisspeptin-10 among them.
BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37 and melanotan II among them. FDA's safety concerns stay posted; withdrawal is not clearance.
FDA staff concluded the criteria weigh against listing BPC-157. Only rulemaking changes the list.

callout.en: Check the live list on the day you prescribe. GHK-Cu alone moved twice in April and May 2026.

text.en: In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, GHK-Cu, LL-37 or melanotan was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026). Copper tripeptide-1 (GHK-Cu) is listed in the Commission's CosIng inventory as a cosmetic ingredient with a skin-conditioning function (read 25 September 2026).

In Portugal, no medicine containing BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, GHK-Cu, LL-37 or melanotan is listed in INFARMED's Infomed register, which includes authorised, lapsed and revoked products (searched 25 September 2026).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that BPC-157 and TB-500 are not authorised as food supplements, and that peptide products such as GHK-Cu, BPC-157, and TB-500 that promise aesthetic effects or improvement in health conditions are not registered with ANVISA. No registered medicine containing KPV, LL-37 or melanotan was found in ANVISA's register (25 September 2026).

In the UAE, no registered product containing BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, LL-37, GHK-Cu or melanotan was found in the register of the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (searched 25 September 2026). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH puts systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides under enhanced controls (31 July 2026) and requires facilities to prohibit the import, distribution, marketing or use of Melanotan II (2 July 2025).

body.en: Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, whether or not it is chemically synthesized, so anything above the line is a biological product. On that date tesamorelin, a 44-residue GHRH analogue, and the enzyme hyaluronidase moved to biologics licences, and FDA told compounders that transitioned biologics cannot use the 503A or 503B exemptions.

blocks.sourceNote: 85 FR 10057 (2020) · FDA notice to compounders, March 2020 · FDA deemed-BLA list · Eli Lilly v. Kennedy (S.D. Ind. 2025; 7th Cir. No. 26-1301)

label.en: amino acids: above this, FDA treats the molecule as a protein, and so as a biological product

detail.en: 85 FR 10057, effective 23 March 2020 · tesamorelin (44 residues) and hyaluronidase moved to biologics licences

means.en: Size decides the rulebook. Peptides of 40 or fewer alpha amino acids stay drugs, so the 503A questions apply; above 40 the product is a biologic, and the compounding exemptions are closed to it.

doesNot.en: It does not make a short peptide lawful to compound; BPC-157 (15 residues) and GHK (3) still need a 503A route. How residues are counted can be contested: a court upheld FDA's count of 39 for retatrutide in 2025, and the appeal was still open at the latest filings (June 2026).

text.en: In the EU, tesamorelin has no marketing authorisation: the application for Egrifta, for excess abdominal fat in HIV patients with lipodystrophy, was withdrawn on 21 June 2012, when the provisional view of EMA's human-medicines committee (CHMP) was that it could not be approved.
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing tesamorelin, including Egrifta, was found in ANVISA's register or online search (25 September 2026).

In the UAE, no registered product containing tesamorelin, and none named Egrifta, was found in the register of the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (searched 25 September 2026).

title.en: Outside the US, 503A does not apply.

body.en: FDA's 503A bulks list and its categories are US law and policy and apply only in the US. In the other jurisdictions in this course, a medicine without a marketing authorisation reaches a patient as a pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply made on a prescription, and the prescriber answers for that choice.

value.en: A pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply

note.en: Made or supplied on a prescription, for a product with no marketing authorisation in that jurisdiction.
The prescriber answers for choosing a medicine without a marketing authorisation.

callout.en: A 503A category means nothing outside the US: name the route your own law provides, and check it on the day.

text.en: The UK handles unlicensed medicines by a different route. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may be supplied to meet one patient's special needs, made to a prescriber's specification by a manufacturer that holds a specials licence, and it may not be advertised. The route (regulation 167): One patient, one prescriber, an unsolicited order. Made to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse or pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under their direct care. No advertisement may be published. Who makes it: A manufacturer with a specials licence. The site is inspected for good manufacturing practice; the product itself is otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy. A pharmacist may also prepare a medicine in a registered pharmacy against a prescription. Special need: The patient's clinical need. MHRA's examples include an intolerance or allergy to an ingredient, or an inability to swallow solid doses. Cost, convenience and operational needs do not count. MHRA's order of preference: Licensed, then off-label, then imported, then special. A UK-licensed medicine comes first, even used off-label; then one licensed in its country of origin; then a UK special. Least acceptable are products that are not medicines where they are made, such as supplements. Responsibility: The prescriber's. Be satisfied the evidence supports safety and efficacy, take responsibility for the prescription and the follow-up, record your reasons, and explain them to the patient when the use is not routine. GMC, MHRA and GPhC guidance say this; nurse prescribers work within the NMC Code. Cost and convenience never justify a special, and a licensed option that meets the need comes first. In the EU, a member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)). Medicines prepared in a pharmacy on prescription for an individual patient (magistral formulas) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formulas) are outside the Directive and need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).

In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use (Circular 148/CD, 29 July 2011), but it may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento). A physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004).

In Brazil, unregistered medicines may be imported only exceptionally, for strictly personal use and on a medical prescription, and import by any route is suspended when ANVISA publishes a specific prohibition; ANVISA stated in September 2025 that using an unregistered imported medicine is entirely the responsibility of the patient and the prescribing physician. ANVISA also stated in November 2024 that compounded medicines should be used only when the registered industrial product is unavailable in the dose or dosage form the patient needs.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 exempts products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies from marketing approval (Art. 5(2)) and lets a physician prescribe a product never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval only when necessary, with no equivalent alternative available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need that no suitable licensed product meets, and where permitted it limits prescribing to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and dispensing by compounding pharmacies to individual prescriptions. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026).

title.en: What a certificate can and cannot prove.

body.en: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own report on a named lot. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate prints the expected mass beside the observed one. HPLC gives purity as a percentage, which says nothing about what the impurities are. Endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results complete it. A certificate cannot prove that the vial in your hand came from that lot, how it was stored since, or that it is sterile and suitable to inject.

points.en: Identity: mass spectrometry, observed against expected
Purity: an HPLC percentage, impurities unnamed
Suitability to inject needs sterility, endotoxin and the right lot

blocks.sourceNote: Peptide Pocket Guide, peptide fundamentals · FDA PCAC briefing, BPC-157 (July 2026) · FDA endotoxin guidance (2026) · Popławska 2019

body.en: Mass spectrometry confirms the molecule's mass. A serious certificate prints the expected mass beside the observed one. In one seized vial, high-resolution mass spectrometry found an undocumented analogue of a known peptide.
HPLC gives the main peak as a percentage. When FDA's reviewers looked at public BPC-157 certificates, most reported purity alone, with no impurity limits.

The acceptable endotoxin level is calculated from the product's dose and route, so a figure without that context proves little. The certificate a BPC-157 nominator sent FDA mentioned no endotoxin test.

audioScript.en: Picture the certificate a patient hands you, and read it line by line, asking what each line actually tests. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate shows the expected mass next to the one measured. HPLC reports purity as a percentage of the main peak, which tells you how much else is present and nothing about what that something else is. Endotoxin matters for anything injected, and FDA's guidance says the acceptable limit is calculated from the dose and the route, so a bare figure settles little. When FDA reviewed BPC-157 for its advisory committee, most public certificates listed purity alone, and the one a nominator supplied mentioned no endotoxin test. Then remember what paper cannot do. A certificate describes a lot. It cannot show that your vial came from that lot, how the vial was stored, or that it is sterile.

title.en: Research use only is a label, and never a route.

body.en: In the US, 'not for use in humans' labelling lets a supplier ship an investigational drug for laboratory or in-vitro research, and obliges the shipper to check that is how it will be used. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions. A certificate cannot turn such a product into a pharmaceutical.

Intended use is read from how a product is sold
A certificate cannot convert a research product

body.en: The US rule lets a supplier ship a drug for laboratory or in-vitro research when the label says it is not for use in humans.
FDA reads what a product is for from its claims, marketing and how it is sold, so a disclaimer on a vial sold for injection carries no weight.

audioScript.en: Research use only sounds like a category. In law it works as a shipping permission. The US rule lets a supplier send an investigational drug for laboratory or test-tube work if the label says it must stay out of people, and the shipper is meant to confirm that is how it will be used. FDA judges what a product is for by how it is marketed and sold, so a disclaimer on a vial offered with injection instructions carries no weight. The Hormonaly guides say it plainly. Research use only is not a clinical pathway. A certificate of analysis, however clean, cannot convert that vial into a pharmaceutical, because sterility, manufacturing standards and a lawful route are all still missing. Whatever your role, treat these products as outside clinical care, and write down exactly what you were told.

prescriber.en: Do not prescribe, supply, supervise or recommend a research-use-only product, and do not read its certificate as permission. Record the product, lot and supplier the patient names, and your advice to stop.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient brings a research-use-only vial or its certificate, record the product name, lot and supplier exactly as printed, do not handle or administer it, and tell the prescriber the same day.

advisor.en: You can explain what a certificate does and does not show. You cannot vouch for a research product, and anyone injecting one should see a prescriber.

text.en: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where it could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)). The Directive's research exclusion covers medicinal products intended for research and development trials (Article 3(3)).

In Portugal, a medicine is any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings or its symptoms, or which may be used in or administered to human beings to make a medical diagnosis or to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento). Making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisations or registrations is an administrative offence punishable by a fine from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category (food, medicine, cosmetic or food supplement) and so are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use. ANVISA also stated in July 2026 that an investigational medicine is used only in authorised clinical research.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 has, since 2 January 2025, barred importing, distributing, possessing, selling, displaying or using any medical product without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023. title.en: Selling and advertising peptides outside the US.

body.en: Outside the US, whether a peptide is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, not on the category a seller chooses, and a medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's prior approval.

points.en: Medicine or not: what is claimed, and what it is and does
No marketing authorisation: no sale, supply or advertising
Prescription-only: public advertising banned or approved first

body.en: Regulators look at what is claimed for a product and at what it is and does. A research-use label or a cosmetic box does not settle it.

audioScript.en: Selling a peptide outside the United States starts with one question, whether the product is a medicine, and regulators answer it from the product itself. They look at what is claimed for it and at what it is and does, so a research-use label or a cosmetic box settles nothing. A medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's approval first, and that covers posts on social media by clinics and influencers. The details differ from country to country, so check the rules for your own jurisdiction, shown with this moment, and date what you find.

text.en: In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicine from its claims, including websites and social media, and from its form and the way it is used. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. MHRA classes injectable melanotan products as medicines, and its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. Prescription-only medicines may not be advertised to the public at all: a clinic may promote 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' without naming the medicine, and in February 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled that influencer posts tagging a weight-loss injection were adverts for a prescription-only medicine. GMC guidance requires doctors to examine a patient physically before prescribing an injectable cosmetic medicine.

In the EU, member states must prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and any advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public, where advertising includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 86 to 88). EU audiovisual law also bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU).

In Portugal, advertising a medicine without a valid national authorisation or registration, or one authorised under Articles 92 and 93, is prohibited, prescription-only medicines may be advertised only in technical media for health professionals, and the advertiser, the agency, anyone disseminating the advertising and the owner of the medium are all liable (Estatuto do Medicamento). Health advertising practices fall under Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects and is enforced by the Health Regulatory Authority (ERS).

In Brazil, advertising of prescription-only medicines on the internet must be accessible exclusively to professionals authorised to prescribe or dispense them, through an electronic registration system (RDC 96/2008), and ANVISA restated in November 2024 that advertising compounded products to the public is not permitted. CFM Resolution 2.336/2023 forbids physicians to promote medicines not registered with ANVISA, and ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category and so are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use.

In the UAE, advertising or promoting any medical product by any means, social media included, needs approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and advertising controlled or semi-controlled products to the public is prohibited (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, Art. 44); an EDE advertising licence requires a valid EDE marketing authorisation for the product, apart from products exempted under Article 5(3) of Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. In Dubai, the DHA bans misleading or unproven peptide claims, such as anti-ageing, cell regeneration or improved appearance, unless the use is approved within the product's regulatory status, and requires any promotion of unregistered materials, including through influencers, to stop (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH bars advertising peptide therapies without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (31 July 2026), and its compounding standard (August 2026) bars advertising emerging, non-monographed substances to patients or professionals.

A peptide that was never approved has no labelling to depart from. The Peptide Pocket Guide names prescribing it for what it is, use of an unapproved drug.
A 503A or 503B product is also unapproved. It is lawful only when the substance and the pharmacy meet the statute's conditions.

audioScript.en: Off-label is the phrase to get right first. FDA uses it for an approved drug prescribed outside its labelling, which prescribers generally may do when they judge it medically appropriate. The idea assumes a label exists. A peptide that was never approved has none, so prescribing it counts as using an unapproved drug, and the Peptide Pocket Guide says exactly that. Compounding leaves that answer unchanged. A compounded product is unapproved by definition, and it is lawful only when the substance and the pharmacy meet the statute's conditions. Under federal law, putting an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act, and in 2020 FDA warned a compounding pharmacy about its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products on that basis. So write the real category in the chart, every time.

text.en: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)). A member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise (Estatuto do Medicamento), and INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians keep the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they judge that, for a given patient, benefits outweigh risks, while no medicine may be manufactured, sold or supplied before it is registered (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12). In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 lets a physician prescribe a medical product for a use not in its leaflet, or one never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function, and where it could also fall under another product law, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)); anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)). In Portugal, a physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004), and a patient-specific exceptional-use authorisation (AUE) always needs an individual clinical justification that the medicine is indispensable (Deliberação 840/2023, 31 August 2023).

In Abu Dhabi, the DoH requires a documented eligibility assessment before peptide therapy and documented informed consent covering expected benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (31 July 2026). why.en: GRADE rates a body of evidence, never one study on its own.

prompt.en: Under section 503A, in what order does the statute let a bulk substance qualify for compounding?

text.en: The bulks list first, then a monograph, then a component of an approved drug.

why.en: Reversed. The bulks list is the last route, open only when the first two are not.

text.en: A USP or NF monograph first, then a component of an approved drug, then the 503A bulks list, with a valid certificate of analysis in every case.

why.en: Correct. The routes are hierarchical, and the certificate and a registered manufacturer are conditions throughout.

text.en: Any substance whose certificate of analysis shows high purity.

why.en: A certificate is a condition, never a route on its own.

rationale.en: The statute's routes are hierarchical, and as of September 2026 no peptide sits on the six-substance bulks list.

answer.en: GRADE rates certainty for a specific outcome across a body of evidence: high, moderate, low or very low (the Hormonaly guides print A to D). Randomized trials start high; certainty drops for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias. Industry-sponsored studies more often report favourable results (Cochrane, 2017), so ask who ran and paid for the trials. A grade is separate from legal status: check both, and never let a mechanism raise a grade. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice.

In the US, a 503A pharmacy may compound only from a substance that meets a USP or NF monograph, or else is a component of an approved drug, or else is on the 503A bulks list (six substances, none a peptide, as of September 2026), and it needs a valid certificate of analysis. A certificate is the supplier's report on one lot: mass spectrometry for identity, HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin and microbial results. It cannot prove your vial is that lot, how it was stored, or that it is sterile or lawful. 'Research use only' products are labelled not for use in humans, and 'off-label' applies only to approved drugs. In the UK, an unlicensed medicine reaches a patient as a 'special', made by a licensed specials manufacturer to a prescriber's order for one patient's special clinical need, or as a medicine a pharmacist prepares against a prescription; MHRA guidance ranks a UK-licensed medicine, even used off-label, ahead of an unlicensed one, and specials may not be advertised. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; for an individual patient, that is the prescriber's decision.
